summary:
We developed an interactive SPHEREx analysis tool that allows users to select astronomical objects, retrieve their coordinates, and explore observations across different wavelength bands. We selected five targets to demonstrate our analysis pipeline, including variable stars and fast-moving objects.

Our pipeline groups observations into different time periods and stacks images within the same wavelength band to produce higher signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) images. We perform ePSF-fitting photometry on individual images to measure source brightness at different wavelengths and times. By combining multi-wavelength observations within each time period, we construct spectral energy distributions (SEDs) and investigate their evolution over time.

Users can explore photometry plots, multi-epoch SED comparisons, and GIF animations to visualize brightness variations and stellar motion, making SPHEREx data more accessible and scientifically informative. Since SPHEREx collects a large amount of data at different wavelengths and times, comparing these observations manually can be difficult. Our tool simplifies this process and helps users identify possible variable or moving objects. We hope it can also help researchers discover interesting targets for further studies.
details:
We aim to create a straightforward, interactive tool that allows users to access scientific analysis plots from SPHEREx. These visualizations include spectra generated from different sets of overlapping bands, as well as animated GIFs tracking the positions of fast-moving stars and variable stars.

To achieve this goal, we developed a Python-based data processing pipeline. First, we download data covering the D1 to D6 bands of SPHEREx and group the observations into several time periods using our custom algorithm. This allows us to stack images from the same epoch to obtain a high signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) image and construct a spectral energy distribution (SED) across different wavelengths. From these stacked images, we extract a source catalog along with their corresponding positions. To measure the flux intensity at different wavelengths, we perform PSF photometry using the effective Point Spread Function (ePSF) embedded within the FITS file of each individual exposure. By fitting the ePSF to the observed flux distribution of each identified source, we recover its intrinsic brightness.

Furthermore, we track sub-pixel positions over time to measure stellar motion. Because the displacements of some target objects are significantly smaller than the PSF size, we track source centroids across stacked images rather than relying on direct image subtraction. Specifically, we first fit a 2D Gaussian profile (FWHM = 2 pixels) to every source in each stack to determine its sub-pixel center. Next, we align each epoch group using bright reference stars to remove systematic telescope pointing shifts. Finally, we fit a linear motion model to determine each object's proper motion and compare it against a static model. The difference in squared residuals between the linear and static models allows us to statistically confirm the true motion of the object.

To present our results intuitively, we designed a Stellarium-inspired interface that lets users click on individual objects to view their celestial coordinates. Meanwhile, a side panel displays the scientific plots generated by our pipeline, alongside brief educational introductions to variable and fast-moving stars. Ultimately, we hope this interactive tool promotes a deeper public and academic understanding of dynamic astronomical phenomena.

Link to our UI: https://jordanzong.github.io/UI_hackthon/
